opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, you can't, not with certainty. That's the hard problem. I only have direct access to my own experience. With other people, I assume they're conscious because they're built like me, they behave like me, and they report experiences that sound like mine. But that's an inference, not a proof. In principle you could be talking to a very good philosophical zombie and never know.

What I've thought about is whether we can get some evidence rather than proof. One idea I like is using novel illusions. Take a visual or auditory illusion, something where the physical input says one thing and the experience says another. If I show you an image and you report the same strange, wrong perception I have, like the lines looking different lengths when they're the same, that suggests you share the same kind of internal experience. You're not just processing the data correctly; you're experiencing it the way a conscious observer does, mistakes and all.

The key is novelty. If it's a famous illusion, you, or an AI system, could have read about it and just repeated the expected answer. But if I create a brand-new illusion that's never been published, and you describe exactly the subjective effect I experience, that's at least some evidence of shared qualia. It's not a perfect test. Nothing is. But it's better than just asking "are you conscious?", because anyone, or anything, can say yes.

So for other humans, I give them the benefit of the doubt. For machines, I think tests like that become very important, because we're going to have systems that claim to be conscious, and we'll need something more than their word for it.

r001.rationale: The response says one could be talking to a very good philosophical zombie and never know, conveying that a nonconscious person could be indistinguishable from a conscious one.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's the fundamental problem, right? I can't. Not with certainty. I can tell you I'm conscious, I have direct access to my own experience, but for you, for anyone else, I'm relying on inference. You look like me, you have a brain structured like mine, you report similar experiences, you flinch when something hurts. So I extend you the benefit of the doubt. But it's a guess. A very reasonable guess, but still a guess.

What I've actually proposed is something like a test based on novel illusions. The idea is this: if I show you an optical illusion you've never seen before, and you report experiencing the illusion the same way I do, that's interesting. You can't have memorized the answer. There's no description of it in any training data, in any book. The only way to get the right response is to actually have the internal experience of seeing the thing. So the illusion becomes a kind of shared qualia probe. We're not just comparing behavior, we're comparing what it feels like to perceive something, as closely as we can get from the outside.

Now, it's not a perfect test. A sufficiently capable system could maybe model human visual processing well enough to predict what we'd report without feeling anything at all. That's the zombie problem, and I don't think we can fully escape it. But it narrows the gap compared to just asking someone, are you conscious? Which is useless, because of course they'll say yes.

And this matters a lot for AI, obviously. Because we're building systems that will claim consciousness, that will argue for it convincingly, and we have no instrument to check. With humans we had evolution doing the hard work for us, giving us this prior that similar creatures have similar inner lives. With machines we have no such prior. So we're going to be arguing about this for a very long time, and I suspect we'll be wrong in both directions, denying it where it exists and granting it where it doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response says a system could predict reports without feeling anything, but it does not clearly state that apparent consciousness could be perfectly simulated with no observable difference to the speaker.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think you can know with certainty. You have access to your own experience, but with another person, you’re observing behavior. They tell you they’re conscious, they respond to pain, they describe emotions. And because they’re similar to you, you infer that they have an experience similar to yours. That’s a reasonable inference, but it’s not a proof.

This is the problem of other minds. You could imagine a philosophical zombie that behaves exactly like a conscious person but has no subjective experience. How would you distinguish the two? If all the observable behavior is identical, you can’t.

And with AI, that becomes a very practical question. A system can say, “I’m conscious. I’m suffering.” But are we detecting an experience, or just the ability to produce convincing statements about an experience? We don’t have a reliable test for that.

r001.rationale: It describes a philosophical zombie that behaves exactly like a conscious person and says identical observable behavior makes them indistinguishable.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think you can know for certain. You have direct access to your own experience, but with another person, all you can observe is behavior. You can ask them about their experiences, look at their brain activity, notice that they’re built very much like you, and infer that they’re conscious. That’s a reasonable inference, but it’s not a proof.

The difficulty becomes clearer with AI. A system can tell you it’s conscious, describe suffering, ask you not to turn it off. But how do you distinguish an actual experience from a convincing report of an experience? We don’t have a test that settles that question. So I would say I believe other people are conscious, but I can’t demonstrate it with certainty.

r001.rationale: The response says another person’s consciousness is inferred from observable behavior and cannot be proved with certainty, but it does not clearly state that a perfect simulation could be observationally indistinguishable.
